![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224989/assets/94b8650466747f6858b30adbb8962e6c91159466b570f536d4999e2b08c31b67.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{1}{2},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224989/assets/cb569d4b7b76699259d2167b8c930e636e3fb794b14ef25a4d909c224235d7c3.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{1}{2}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$
